findings.issue: A refund.failed that arrives for a row already SUCCEEDED only logs at WARN ('conflicting ... ignored'). The design names this exact rollout case: an old pod inserts the refund with the SUCCEEDED default, then Razorpay sends refund.failed. The customer is then unpaid while the system shows the refund as done, and the only signal is a warn line that operators are expected to grep for. The ERROR-level alert that should cover a customer who was not refunded never fires.
findings.fix: When current is SUCCEEDED and target is FAILED, log at ERROR with a greppable prefix (for example 'REFUND FAILED AFTER SUCCEEDED') that includes the order id, refund id and amount. Keep the no-overwrite rule (AC-6) and change no state.

findings.issue: findRefundByProviderRefundId uses a non-unique index with ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1. The design says the handler warns when more than one row matches, but the code silently takes the oldest row. If duplicates ever exist, the wrong refund row could be settled or released, and nobody would be told.
findings.fix: Count the matches, or select LIMIT 2. If more than one row matches, log at ERROR and apply nothing. Alternatively, add a partial UNIQUE index in a later migration once production data has been checked for duplicates.

findings.issue: On FAILED, `p.refundedAmount().subtract(r.amount()).max(BigDecimal.ZERO)` hides a negative result. A negative value means the ledger is already inconsistent, and this code writes 0 without saying anything.
findings.fix: If the subtraction goes below zero, log at ERROR (ledger inconsistency) before clamping, or refuse to apply the change.

findings.issue: Migration locking: (1) the inline CHECK constraint on the new column makes Postgres scan the whole of payment.refunds to validate it while holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. (2) CREATE INDEX ix_payments_provider_payment is not CONCURRENTLY, so writes to payment.payments, the hot money table, are blocked while the index builds. This is acceptable at current table sizes but is not zero-downtime.
findings.fix: Either state the expected table sizes and lock duration in the runbook/rollout note, or split the change: add the CHECK as NOT VALID and then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, and build the payments index CONCURRENTLY in a non-transactional Flyway migration.

findings.issue: Parked events that fail validation inside refund() are deleted and only warned about. Their event id is already in processed_events, so Razorpay will not redeliver them. The refund then stays PENDING with no settlement path until the stuck-PENDING alert arrives in slice 2.
findings.fix: Log a dropped parked mismatch at ERROR. Alternatively, keep the parked row (do not delete it) when validation fails, so an operator can reconcile it by hand.

summary: I approve slice 1 with minor findings only; I found no blocker or major issue. No new endpoints are added. Refund events go through the existing HMAC signature gate (RazorpayGateway.verifyWebhookSignature, constant-time MessageDigest.isEqual) before the refund.* branch, and a bad signature records nothing. A forged event cannot move money. A replayed or duplicated signed event also cannot move money twice: settling is a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='PENDING', so a refund is released at most once. That holds even when the X-Razorpay-Event-Id header, which the signature does not cover, is changed to slip past processed_events, because the second delivery finds the refund already settled and does nothing. The released amount comes from our own refund row, never from the payload. The payload's payment id, amount in minor units and currency must all match before anything is applied, and a payment-id or refund-row mismatch is ignored. Only rows with a provider_refund_id can be touched, so Stripe, COD, wallet and historic SUCCEEDED rows cannot be flipped. Locking is sound. The webhook and refund() both take the payments row lock first, so under READ COMMITTED a parked event is always seen by one side or the other. Concurrent deliveries are serialised by the payment lock together with the processed_events primary key, and the whole handler runs in one transaction, so a failure rolls back the event record and Razorpay retries. Two refunds pending at once each release only their own amount, and a FAILED release puts the payment back to its correct earlier status (SUCCEEDED or PARTIALLY_REFUNDED). All SQL uses bound parameters, so I found no injection path. Logs contain only Razorpay ids, internal UUIDs, order ids and amounts: no PII, secrets or raw payloads. No dependencies are added. The minors are about making operators see problems: an ERROR alert when refund.failed arrives after SUCCEEDED, a warning for duplicate provider_refund_id rows, a warning when the balance clamp hides a ledger inconsistency, migration lock behaviour on payments/refunds, and parked mismatches being dropped quietly. Two older risks were not introduced by this change and are out of scope: Razorpay is called outside the local transaction, and it is unproven whether Razorpay honours X-Refund-Idempotency (design Q3).
